946.title: The Light of Asia
946.hook: Edwin Arnold's long poem of the Buddha's life, told in English verse
946.carry: a dewdrop slipping into the shining sea
946.howItsDone: The Light of Asia is no longer a scripture anyone practices from, but it is still read as literature, and some Western Buddhists and readers of Buddhism remember it as the book that first introduced them to the Buddha's life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Max Müller and the translators who carried the texts into French and English. Your line was into English. What word did you catch that didn't cross over exactly? Day nine hundred forty-six.

What happens when the Buddha's story leaves the scholar's desk and lands in a parlor? A translation of the Dhammapada is careful, scholarly work. But an English poet and newspaperman named Edwin Arnold had a different idea. He would tell the whole life of the Buddha as a long poem: the palace, the four sights, the night he left, the tree, the awakening, the teaching. In English verse, for ordinary readers. He gave it a title. Today, Edwin Arnold.
screen: `FROM THE DESK TO THE PARLOR.` → `A WHOLE LIFE AS A POEM.` → `FOR ORDINARY READERS.`

segments.voice: First, what it is. The Light of Asia is not a translation of any one scripture. It's an original English poem, in long, rolling lines, that draws on the traditional stories of the Buddha's life. Its subtitle calls it The Great Renunciation, and Arnold presents it as told by an Indian Buddhist, so the voice is meant to be a believer's, speaking with love. Second, what it tells. The young prince Siddhartha grows up in a palace where sorrow is hidden from him. He sees age, sickness, death, and a wandering holy man. He leaves his sleeping wife and child in the night. He searches, nearly starves, sits beneath the tree, and wakes up. Then he teaches. The story is one this path has told already, but the poem tells it with color: gardens, music, horses, moonlight. Third, the last image. Near the poem's end, after the teaching of nirvana, Arnold leaves the reader with a picture: a dewdrop slipping into the shining sea. A small, bright thing, letting go of its edges, and becoming part of something vast. Readers have argued about whether that's what nirvana means, and Buddhist teachers explain it in different ways. But the picture stayed with people. Fourth, why it mattered. For some readers in Britain and America, this poem was their first meeting with the Buddha at all, not as a curiosity but as a teacher worth loving. It's long and old-fashioned, and critics have called it more Victorian than Indian in places. And yet it carried the story into homes the scholars never reached.
screen: `AN ORIGINAL POEM, NOT A SCRIPTURE.` · `THE PRINCE, THE NIGHT, THE TREE.` · `A DEWDROP SLIPS INTO THE SEA.` · `INTO HOMES THE SCHOLARS NEVER REACHED.` · then, large: `THE LIGHT OF ASIA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read a few lines of it. The poem is old enough to be free to read, and after the bell you can find its opening, or its ending, and read a few lines aloud. For now, settle, and breathe. Take Arnold's last picture with you: a single dewdrop, bright on a leaf. On each out-breath, let it slip a little closer to the water. You don't need to decide what it means. Just let the small thing rest in the large one. The bell holds the time.
Edwin Arnold. The English poet who told the Buddha's life in verse, ending with a dewdrop slipping into the shining sea. Today's word.
Your line: a dewdrop slipping into the shining sea. Today, read something aloud to someone, a poem, a page, a paragraph, and let a story travel by voice. Day nine hundred forty-six.

947.title: Chicago, 1893
947.hook: at the World's Parliament of Religions, Dharmapala and the Zen teacher Soyen Shaku speak
947.howItsDone: Buddhists in Sri Lanka honor Anagarika Dharmapala as a reviver of the teaching and of the sites in India, and Japanese Zen remembers Soyen Shaku as a teacher who brought Zen before Western listeners.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a long poem carried the Buddha's life to English readers. Your line was a dewdrop slipping into the shining sea. Did one of its pictures stay with you? Day nine hundred forty-seven.
screen: `A DEWDROP SLIPPING INTO THE SHINING SEA.`

segments.voice: A big hall in Chicago, with a long row of speakers on the stage. People of many faiths have been invited to stand up, one after another, and explain their own tradition to a crowd of strangers. Some in the seats have read about the Buddha in books like the poem we met yesterday. Now a Buddhist is standing in front of them. A young man from Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, in a plain white robe: Anagarika Dharmapala. And beside him on the program, a Zen abbot from Japan named Soyen Shaku. Today, the teaching steps up to the podium and speaks for itself.
screen: `A HALL IN CHICAGO.` → `FAITHS ON ONE STAGE.` → `TWO BUDDHIST VOICES.`

segments.voice: First, the gathering. It was called the World's Parliament of Religions, and it met alongside a great fair in Chicago. Its organizers wanted the religions of the world side by side, each speaking in its own words, and they printed the speeches afterward, so we can still read them. Second, Dharmapala. He had spent his young life working to restore Buddhist places in India, above all Bodh Gaya, where the Buddha woke up under the tree. In Chicago he spoke about the Buddha as a teacher of reason and kindness, whose way was open to anyone willing to practice it. Third, Soyen Shaku. He was the abbot of a Zen temple in Kamakura, and he did not speak English. His talk, on cause and effect, was put into English and read to the hall for him. Accounts say a young lay student of his helped with the English. That student's name was D. T. Suzuki, and he comes back tomorrow. Fourth, why it matters. Some in that hall had met the Buddha only in books by outsiders, like yesterday's poem. Here, Buddhists were speaking for themselves. The Dhammapada has a line that fits a week of long speeches: "Even though a speech be a thousand (of words), but made up of senseless words, one word of sense is better, which if a man hears, he becomes quiet." One word of sense. In a hall full of speeches, that was the hope.
screen: `A PARLIAMENT OF RELIGIONS.` · `DHARMAPALA SPEAKS.` · `SOYEN SHAKU, IN ENGLISH.` · `ONE WORD OF SENSE.` · then, large: `THE TEACHING SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one sentence about your own practice, said out loud. Quietly is fine. Not a speech, just one true sentence. It might be, I sit for a couple of minutes most days. Or, I'm learning what the Buddha taught. Or, I'm still working out what my practice is. Whatever is true for you today. Say it once, slowly. Then stop talking, close your eyes, and sit in the quiet that comes after it, the way the Dhammapada says one word of sense leaves the hearer quiet. The bell holds the time.
Chicago. Where, at a parliament of faiths, Dharmapala and Soyen Shaku stood up and spoke for the Buddha's teaching in their own voices. Today's word.
Your line: the teaching speaks. Today, if someone asks what you've been learning, give them one honest sentence instead of a speech, and then let them answer. Day nine hundred forty-seven.

948.title: Zen comes west
948.hook: teachers like D. T. Suzuki carry Zen to Western readers
948.howItsDone: Zen communities in the West sit together in meditation halls, often under teachers trained in Japan or in lineages that came from there, and read short Zen stories as part of their study.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chicago, and two Buddhist voices on one stage. Your line was the teaching speaks. What was your one sentence? Day nine hundred forty-eight.

A story told in Zen circles. A learned visitor comes to a Zen teacher to ask about Zen. The teacher serves tea. He pours into the visitor's cup until it's full, and keeps pouring. Tea runs over the rim and across the table. Stop, says the visitor, it's full, nothing more will go in. Like this cup, the teacher answers, you are full of your own opinions. How can I show you Zen unless you first empty your cup? Stories like that one crossed the ocean in books, and some Western readers met Zen first on the page. Today, Suzuki.
screen: `A CUP OF TEA.` → `IT OVERFLOWS.` → `FIRST, EMPTY YOUR CUP.`

segments.voice: First, the student. Yesterday we met a young layman who helped the Zen abbot Soyen Shaku with his English in Chicago. D. T. Suzuki had trained in Zen under that abbot in Kamakura. Afterward he went to America and spent years there translating and writing. Second, the books. Suzuki wrote about Zen in English, in essays and translations, and later he lectured to university audiences. Readers who had never met a Zen teacher met Zen through him: the sudden awakenings, the strange questions, the teachers who answered with a shout. Third, the stories. What crossed the ocean most easily were the short stories, like the cup of tea. Zen describes itself with a saying tradition gives to Bodhidharma, whom we met on the road through China: a special transmission outside the scriptures, not depending on words, pointing straight at the mind. There's a gentle joke in that. A tradition that says it does not depend on words reached the West through a great many of them. Fourth, the cushion. Zen keeps pointing past the book. The stories are meant to unsettle the mind that thinks it already knows, and the tradition's answer to that unsettled mind is to sit. So the books were followed by people. Japanese teachers came to the West to lead sittings, and Western students went to Japan to train in monasteries and came home to teach. A cup of tea in a book, and then real cups of tea at real meditation halls, across the ocean.
screen: `SUZUKI, A STUDENT OF ZEN.` · `BOOKS IN ENGLISH.` · `STORIES THAT CROSSED.` · `FROM THE BOOK TO THE CUSHION.` · then, large: `ACROSS THE OCEAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one short Zen story, read slowly. You've already heard it: the cup of tea. Go through it once more in your mind. The guest, the pouring, the tea running over, empty your cup. Then set the story down, close your eyes, and meet the next breath as if it were the first one you'd ever noticed. And the next. When the mind starts to say, I know this already, let a little tea spill over the rim, and come back to the breath that's actually here. The bell holds the time.
Suzuki. D. T. Suzuki, the Zen student whose books and lectures carried the teaching to America, and the stories like the cup of tea. Today's word.
Your line: across the ocean. Today, the next time someone hands you a cup or pours you a drink, let it remind you to listen before you answer. Day nine hundred forty-eight.

949.title: Temples in the West
949.hook: Japanese American temples, including through the wartime internment camps where practice continued
949.howItsDone: Japanese American Buddhist temples, including Jodo Shinshu temples, hold regular services, Sunday schools and a summer Obon festival with dancing, and some communities hold pilgrimages to the sites of the wartime camps.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Suzuki carried Zen west in books and in a cup of tea that overflowed. Your line was across the ocean. Did you leave a little room in the cup? Day nine hundred forty-nine.

A Sunday morning in a plain wooden barracks. Benches in rows. A small altar built by hand, an incense bowl, a priest in robes, and families chanting together. Outside the door: a fence, and a guard tower. During the Second World War, the United States government forced Japanese Americans from their homes on the West Coast and held them in camps. Among the things people carried in with them was their Buddhist practice. And inside the fence, it kept going. Today, the temples that crossed the Pacific, and what they kept through the war years.
screen: `A SERVICE IN A BARRACKS.` → `A FENCE OUTSIDE.` → `PRACTICE KEPT GOING.`

segments.voice: First, the temples. Japanese families who settled in Hawaii and on the American mainland built temples, among them temples of Jodo Shinshu, the Pure Land school of Shinran we met in Japan. These were family temples: services, funerals, Sunday schools for the children, and the summer Obon festival, when the dead are remembered and the community dances together in the street. Second, wartime. When war came between the United States and Japan, Buddhist priests, as community leaders, were among those taken away for questioning and detention. Then whole families, citizens and not, were removed to camps in the interior. Temples were closed, and some families hid or left behind their home altars. Third, practice continued. In the camps people organized Buddhist services, held funerals, ran Sunday schools and youth groups, and danced Obon in the dust between the barracks. They said the nembutsu, the Pure Land phrase Namu Amida Butsu, entrusting themselves to Amida Buddha. Fourth, a name. During those years, at a camp in Utah, the temple association of the mainland took the name Buddhist Churches of America, and it still goes by that name. After the camps closed, families came home, reopened temples, and started again. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's words, has a picture of steadiness that fits these temples: "As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, wise people falter not amidst blame and praise." Wind on every side, and with their temples shut, the communities kept their ground.
screen: `FAMILY TEMPLES IN THE WEST.` · `PRIESTS DETAINED, FAMILIES REMOVED.` · `SERVICES INSIDE THE CAMPS.` · `A NAME THAT STAYED.` · then, large: `PRACTICE CONTINUED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a community that endured. Bring one to mind. It might be the families in these camps, holding services behind a fence. It might be your own family, or a neighborhood, a congregation, a group of friends that came through something hard and kept its practices going. Hold them in mind without needing to say anything about them. If you'd like to make a small gesture, bow your head or put your palms together for a moment. Then sit quietly with them. The bell holds the time.
Jodo Shinshu. The Pure Land school of Shinran, whose family temples in Hawaii and on the mainland kept services, Sunday schools and Obon going, even inside the wartime camps. Today's word.
Your line: kept their ground. Today, if something interrupts your routine, come back to one small piece of it anyway, a breath, a pause, a kind word. Day nine hundred forty-nine.

950.title: Tibetan teachers in exile
950.hook: after 1959 Tibetan teachers settle in India, then teach worldwide
950.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists in exile keep up their monasteries, schools and debate in India and Nepal, and Tibetan teachers lead centers around the world where students study and practice in their lineages.

segments.voice: Yesterday, temples in the West, and services held inside a fence. Your line was kept their ground. What small piece of practice did you come back to? Day nine hundred fifty.

A high mountain pass, snow to the knees, thin air. A monk walks it with a bundle tied to his back: a few long, loose-leaf texts wrapped in cloth, the kind we saw in the Tibetan canons. Behind him are the monasteries where he learned to read them. Ahead, the foothills of India, a country he has never seen. When the Dalai Lama left Tibet for India, monks, nuns, teachers and families followed him over passes like this one, on foot. Today, the teachers who carried a whole tradition into exile, and then out into the world.
screen: `A MOUNTAIN PASS.` → `TEXTS TIED TO HIS BACK.` → `INTO INDIA.`

segments.voice: First, a new home. The Dalai Lama settled in Dharamsala, a hill town in the north of India, and it became the center of Tibetan life in exile, with its own offices, schools, temples and a library for Tibetan texts. Second, monasteries rebuilt. Monks who made it across rebuilt their great monasteries in settlements in southern India, on farmland far from the snow. Sera, Drepung and Ganden, names from the hills around Lhasa, rose again there. The debate courtyards came back too: monks clapping and questioning each other in the afternoon, just as they had at home. Third, out into the world. In exile, teachers met students from everywhere. Lamas from the Nyingma, Kagyu, Sakya and Gelug schools traveled to Europe, North America, Asia and beyond, and founded centers where people who had never seen Tibet learned its chants, its meditations and its texts. Fourth, what they carried. A refugee may have to leave almost everything behind. These teachers carried the teaching in memory, in practice, and in those loose-leaf texts on their backs. In the last year of the Buddha's life, as Rhys Davids' translation of the Book of the Great Decease tells it, he gave this advice to Ananda: "be ye lamps unto yourselves. Be ye a refuge to yourselves." A refuge you can carry. For Tibetan teachers who lost their monasteries, their country and their road home, that is what the teaching had to become, and what they handed on to students they could never have pictured meeting.
screen: `A HOME IN DHARAMSALA.` · `MONASTERIES REBUILT IN INDIA.` · `TEACHERS GO OUT INTO THE WORLD.` · `A REFUGE YOU CAN CARRY.` · then, large: `TEACHING IN EXILE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a refugee. Choose one person: someone you know, a neighbor, a classmate, a coworker, or someone in your own family's story. Or a face from the news, or a monk on a mountain pass. Hold that person in mind. Think of what they had to leave, and what they managed to carry. If you like, silently wish them safety and a place to rest. Then let the picture go, and sit. The bell holds the time.
Dharamsala. The hill town in India where the Dalai Lama settled and Tibetan teachers rebuilt their monasteries and taught the world. Today's word.
Your line: teaching in exile. Today, notice one thing you carry that no one could take from you, a skill, a memory, a habit of kindness, and use it once. Day nine hundred fifty.

951.title: Insight goes west
951.hook: Burmese and Thai meditation methods reach Western lay students
951.howItsDone: Insight meditation students sit and walk in silence, noting what arises, often on retreats at centers in the Burmese or Thai lineages, and Theravada monasteries in the West also teach meditation to laypeople.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dharamsala, and the Tibetan teachers in exile who carried a whole tradition over the mountains. Your line was teaching in exile. What did you carry and use? Day nine hundred fifty-one.

Rising. Falling. Rising. Falling. In a meditation hall in Yangon, a student sits with her attention on her belly, silently naming each movement as the breath comes and goes. A sound outside: hearing. A thought about lunch: thinking. Back to rising, falling. The instruction from her teacher is short: know what is happening, while it's happening. No robes required, no years in a monastery first. That simple method, and other ways of sitting from Burma and Thailand, traveled to lay students on the other side of the world. Today, vipassana.
screen: `RISING, FALLING.` → `HEARING. THINKING.` → `KNOW IT AS IT HAPPENS.`

segments.voice: First, meditation for laypeople. In Burma, teachers began to teach meditation to ordinary laypeople, not only to monks and nuns. Ledi Sayadaw wrote and taught for lay students, and later Mahasi Sayadaw opened a center in Yangon where anyone could come and practice. Second, the method. The Mahasi way is noting: a soft mental label for whatever is happening, moment by moment. It rests on an old teaching, the sutta on the setting up of mindfulness. There, the Buddha says that a practitioner who is walking knows, I am walking, and who is standing knows, I am standing, and so with sitting and lying down. Know the body as body, feelings as feelings, the mind as mind. The Pali for the clear seeing that grows from this is vipassana, insight. Third, the forest. In Thailand, forest monks like Ajahn Chah taught in simple monasteries among the trees. Western men came to him, ordained, and some went on to found monasteries in England and elsewhere. Fourth, the travelers. Western students who had sat in Burma, Thailand and India came home and began teaching insight meditation in plain retreat centers, often to people who called themselves nothing in particular. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's words, opens its chapter on earnestness like this: "Earnestness is the path of immortality (Nirvâna), thoughtlessness the path of death." Rising, falling, hearing, thinking. Small, earnest noting, carried across the world.
screen: `MEDITATION FOR LAYPEOPLE.` · `NOTING, MOMENT BY MOMENT.` · `MONKS OF THE THAI FOREST.` · `STUDENTS CARRY IT HOME.` · then, large: `INSIGHT TRAVELS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: noting. On another day you might give it ten minutes; for now, the bell holds a shorter sit. Sit comfortably. Rest your attention on your belly, and as it moves, note it softly in your mind: rising, falling. If a sound comes, note hearing, then come back. If a thought comes, note thinking, then come back. Keep the labels gentle and short, like a whisper. No need to get it right. Just know what is happening, while it's happening. The bell holds the time.
Vipassana. Insight, the clear seeing taught by Burmese noting and the Thai forest way, carried to laypeople far from Asia. Today's word.
Your line: insight travels. Today, take noting with you. Once, while walking somewhere, note walking, walking, for ten steps, and then carry on. Day nine hundred fifty-one.

952.title: Everywhere now
952.hook: Buddhist communities in Europe, Africa, Latin America and beyond
952.carry: a good man pervades every place
952.howItsDone: Buddhist communities around the world gather in temples, monasteries and meditation centers, from family temples of immigrant communities to centers founded by Western students and temples built abroad by Asian orders.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vipassana went west: rising, falling, hearing, thinking. Your line was insight travels. Did you note ten steps of walking? Day nine hundred fifty-two.

Three postcards. The first, from Brazil: a temple in São Paulo, incense, a family bowing before a Japanese altar, and a conversation in Portuguese afterward over tea. The second, from South Africa: a large temple with curved roofs on the grass near Pretoria, built by a Buddhist order from Taiwan. The third, from Germany: a quiet house on a hill on the northern edge of Berlin, with steps up to a shrine room, where monks from Sri Lanka live. Three continents, one teaching. Today, the end of a week of crossings, and a look at where the road has led.
screen: `A TEMPLE IN SÃO PAULO.` → `A TEMPLE NEAR PRETORIA.` → `A HOUSE IN BERLIN.`

segments.voice: First, families brought temples. When people move, their practice moves with them. Japanese families in Brazil built temples, just as they did in Hawaii and California. Sri Lankan, Thai, Vietnamese, Chinese, Korean and Tibetan communities have done the same in cities across Europe, the Americas, Africa and Australia, sometimes starting in a living room before there was a building. Second, seekers built centers. Others came to the teaching through books and travel. In Berlin, a doctor named Paul Dahlke built a house for Buddhist practice, and it still stands as a temple. Third, orders sent teachers. Some Asian orders built temples abroad on purpose. The Taiwanese order Fo Guang Shan built Nan Hua Temple in South Africa, near Pretoria, and from it monks and nuns have taught in other parts of Africa. Fourth, the week. Look at the road we've walked since the poem. The Light of Asia put the Buddha's life into English verse. In Chicago, the teaching spoke for itself. Zen came west in a cup of tea. Temples kept their practice going behind a fence. Tibetan teachers carried a tradition over the mountains. Insight came west as noting. And today, everywhere now. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's words, compares the good to a scent that goes where flowers can't, and ends the verse like this: "a good man pervades every place." A teaching that began on foot in northern India now has shrine rooms on continents far from where it began.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a community far away. After the bell, if you like, look one up: a temple or sitting group in a country you've never been to. For now, picture one. Choose a place, any place far from where you're sitting. Picture a shrine room there, a small one, with a few people sitting, maybe at this very hour, in a language you don't speak. Breathe in, and know they're breathing too. Breathe out. Sit with them, across the distance. The bell holds the time.
Everywhere now. Temples in São Paulo, near Pretoria and in Berlin, built by families, seekers and orders, far from where the teaching began. Today's word.

Your line: a good man pervades every place. Today, when you pass a place of worship that isn't familiar, notice it, and remember someone there is practicing too. That's the week. Day nine hundred fifty-two.
